newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr stumbles as yen strength continues.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr stumbles as yen strength continues.

text.p: The Australian dollar unwound overnight gains against the U.S. dollar and continued to weaken against the yen on Friday, caught up in U.S. dollar weakness and outright selling against the yen.
Traders said the U.S. dollar market was slightly panicky after comments from Japanese officials that suggested they sought a stronger yen, and this weighed on the local dollar.

By 5.00 p.m. (0700 GMT) the Australian dollar was trading at US$0.7782/87 and 95.64/74 yen, down on an opening US$0.7807/12 and 96.59/69 yen, and compared with closes on Thursday of US$0.7776/81 and 97.08/18 yen.
Traders said there had been outright selling of the Australian dollar against the yen, which has now fallen around 4.5 yen from a five year high above 100 yen last week.

With sentiment turning bearish on the U.S. dollar, a speech from U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan had something for both interest rate bulls and bears and added to the market's confusion, which spread to other dollar bloc currencies.

"(Greenspan) said a lot of things, some of it bullish and some of it bearish, but what's driving the market at the moment is these huge flows that are coming through out of Japanese investors," said Andrew McGill, a forex sales dealer at Chase.
McGill described the market as being in a minor panic, as well established long positions in the dollar were being sold as sentiment on the dollar weakened.
In turn, this meant fundamentals were ignored as traders tried to meet their orders, and the only comments that were making an impact were those specifically on exchange rates.

In his speech, Greenspan said the Fed would need to act if U.S. growth failed to slow as expected, and the economy had little slack now. He saw scant signs of an imminent inflation resurgence, and while modest growth and low inflation was still likely in 1997/98, it was less sure now.
Greenspan defended the March rate hike against what he said was an unusual amount of critcism, and said 1997 was not like 1994 when rates had to be raised sharply to head off inflation.

However, it was concerns the Japanese wanted a stronger yen, and the prospect of combined central bank intervention to achieve this, that was really driving the market, traders said. The comments that were most worrying were those late in Thursday by Eisuke Sakakibara, a senior Japanese Ministry of Finance official, that the yen could strengthen to 103 yen to the dollar.

"103, they're pretty strong words, and unless someone else comes out with another line like that the market's too busy just trying to clear the business that's actually going through," McGill said. The U.S. dollar ended just above 123 yen, recovering from a late dumping when it fell below this level.
"We're having this huge shakeout of offshore investments out of Japan and the market's struggling to obtain the liquidity needed to get that business through," he said.
The dip in the local dollar happened shortly before the midsession and it held fairly steady above US$0.7770 through the afternoon.
This was reflected in the trade weighted index, which held steady at 60.0 through the afternoon, after falling from an opening 60.3.
Traders said while ongoing yen strength would keep the pressure on the Australian dollar, there were some positives for the dollar.

Not only do Australian interest rates appear to be on hold, with a bias towards a tightening, but next Tuesday's budget is expected to be favourably received, and carry on the fiscal consolidation that will see it in surplus by June 1999.
